findings.question: q-statistics-and-probability-measures-of-variability-0005
findings.quote: It is the positive square root of the average squared distance of the values from the mean.
findings.problem: The keyed definition excludes zero, so none of the choices correctly defines population standard deviation for every dataset. For the population 6,6,6,6, the average squared distance is 0 and the standard deviation is 0. Zero has no positive square root. The other choices define range, mode, and median.
findings.fix: Replace “positive square root” with “nonnegative square root”.

findings.question: q-statistics-and-probability-measures-of-variability-0015
findings.quote: So the values sit closer to it than to the true population average, and the calculated spread tends to come out too small. Dividing by $n-1$ instead of $n$ makes the result a little bigger.
findings.problem: The comparison and increase are stated without allowing equality. A random sample 0,2 from the population 0,1,2 has the same mean as the population, so its distances to the two means are equal. Also, a sample 1,1 has zero squared deviations, so dividing by n-1 instead of n leaves the result at 0. Only the total squared distance is minimized at the sample mean; individual values need not be closer to it.
findings.fix: Say that the squared distances add up to no more, and usually less, when measured from the sample average. Say dividing by n-1 raises a positive result and corrects the tendency to underestimate variance over many random samples.
